claim: Palantir Technologies — the data-analytics firm seeded by In-Q-Tel, the CIA's venture-capital arm — ran predictive-policing programs inside US city police departments. In New Orleans, a partnership that began in 2012 gave the New Orleans Police Department (NOPD) software that traced residents' ties to gang members, mined their social media and criminal histories, and predicted the likelihood that individuals "would commit violence or become a victim." The Verge revealed in February 2018 that most of the City Council had never been told: the deal was routed as a pro-bono "philanthropic" arrangement that bypassed procurement and public oversight. In Los Angeles, the LAPD ran Operation LASER (Los Angeles' Strategic Extraction and Restoration), which assigned individuals a points-based "LASER score" to flag them as risks. Los Angeles ended Operation LASER in 2019; New Orleans dropped Palantir within weeks of the 2018 exposé.

sources.label: Type Investigations / The Verge (Ali Winston) — "Did Palantir Secretly Use New Orleans to Test Predictive Policing?" (February 27, 2018). The NOPD partnership, its 2012 start, and the council's ignorance of it.
sources.quote: Key city council members and attorneys contacted by The Verge had no idea that the city had any sort of relationship with Palantir, nor were they aware that Palantir used its program in New Orleans to market its services to another law enforcement agency for a multimillion-dollar contract.

sources.label: The Intercept — "How the LAPD and Palantir Use Data to Justify Racist Policing" (January 30, 2021). Operation LASER, the LASER score, and its 2019 end.
sources.quote: A third program, Operation LASER, which stands for Los Angeles' Strategic Extraction and Restoration program, used a points-based system, called a LASER score, to evaluate the risk that individuals posed.
